title: I want to learn
goal: Say what you want, can, and must do, and use the subjunctive with *să* — the Romanian way of linking two verbs, which replaces the infinitive almost everywhere.
bekal: link two verbs with *să*: *vreau să învăț*, *trebuie să plec*
form the third-person subjunctive: *vorbește → să vorbească*, *merge → să meargă*, *are → să aibă*, *este → să fie*
use *a putea*, *a ști*, and *trebuie să* — and tell "can" (it's possible) from "can" (I know how)

notes: **Vreau să învăț — two verbs, both conjugated.** English says "want to learn" with an infinitive. Romanian links the verbs with *să*, and the second verb still shows who does it: *vreau să învăț, vrei să înveți, vrem să învățăm*. *Vreau a învăța* is not used.

**Ce vrei să facem?** Because the second verb carries its own subject, it can differ from the first: *vrei* (you want) + *să facem* (we do) = "what do you want us to do?". Likewise *Vreau să vorbim* — "I want us to speak".

**Să mă ajuți, să mă ajute.** Short pronouns stand between *să* and the verb. Compare the endings: *mă ajuți* (you), but *doamna Popescu vrea să mă ajute* — third person, and that is where the subjunctive has its own form (*ajută → să ajute*).

**Știi să gătești?** *A ști să* = know how, have the skill. *A putea să* = circumstances allow it. Andrei knows how to get to a kitchen, but *nu poate să vină* — he has an exam. English uses "can" for both; Romanian keeps them apart.
**Vorbește rar.** *Rar* means "rarely" (unit 8), but for speech it means "slowly, unhurried". Hence your lifesaver: *Mai rar, vă rog* — "slower, please".

grammars.title: The subjunctive with să
body: After *vreau, pot, știu, trebuie, îmi place* and many other verbs, Romanian uses **să + a conjugated verb**. The good news: for *eu, tu, noi, voi* the form is **exactly the same as the present tense**. Only the third person has its own form — one form for singular and plural.
The rule: the third-person ending **swaps**. A present ending in *-ă* becomes *-e*; one ending in *-e* becomes *-ă*.
after: **One full verb:** *vreau să merg, vrei să mergi, vrea să meargă, vrem să mergem, vreți să mergeți, vor să meargă*. You've known four of the six forms since unit 8; the other two share one form, *să meargă*.

**A fi is the only one that differs in every person:** *să fiu, să fii, să fie, să fim, să fiți, să fie*. *Vreau să fiu profesor* = "I want to be a teacher". For *a avea*, only the third person is special: *să am, să ai, să aibă*.
**The order after *să* is fixed:** *să* + *nu* + short pronoun + verb. *Vreau să nu lucrez sâmbăta. Poți să nu mă aștepți.* Subjects and time words can't slip in between.

grammars.title: A putea, a ști, and trebuie să
body: The three verbs most often found before *să*. The first two conjugate normally; the third **never changes** — the subject shows only in the verb after *să*.
after: ***Nu trebuie să* means "don't need to"**, not "mustn't": *Nu trebuie să plătești* = "you don't have to pay". To forbid, use *nu poți să…* or *nu se poate*.

**After *a putea*, *să* can be dropped** and replaced by the infinitive without *a*: *Pot veni* = *Pot să vin*; *Puteți repeta?* = *Puteți să repetați?* Both are correct. This is the only verb that often does this; with the others, always use *să*.
*Poate* on its own also means "maybe": *Poate mâine* — "maybe tomorrow". And *Nu știu* ("I don't know") is the most honest sentence you can use any time.

blocks.text: *Se spune* and *se scrie* use the *se* you know from unit 8, but here it means "one says", "one writes" — Romanian's way of making a sentence with no doer, much like the English passive: *Cum se spune?* = "how is it said?". With a friend, *Puteți repeta?* becomes *Poți să repeți?*

blocks.title: Romanian: a friendly distant cousin
items: Romanian is a Romance language — in the same family as Italian, Spanish, and French — that grew out of Latin on Europe's eastern edge. That's why so many words feel familiar to an English speaker: *problemă, familie, muzică, examen, corect*.
Its Slavic neighbors left their mark on everyday words: *da* (yes), *prieten* (friend), *a iubi* (to love). The same language is also the official language of the Republic of Moldova.
Romanians rarely meet foreigners who want to learn their language, so your three halting sentences are usually met with a big smile and a *Bravo!*

Meaning

can, have time — I can come.
can, know how — I can swim.

head: Third person — this is where the form changes
English
rows: Ioana wants to go to the seaside.
*Copiii trebuie să fie acasă la opt.*
The children must be home at eight.
They want to have a car.

blocks.title: Să without a lead verb
items: *Să* can also open a sentence on its own. With *noi* it becomes a suggestion: *Să mergem!* (Let's go!), *Să vedem* (Let's see).
In questions it expresses doubt: *Ce să fac?* — "What should I do?". And in wishes: *Să ai o zi bună!* — "Have a nice day!"
